turns.learner: Hello teacher. I want to practise rules, like what you must and mustn't do at school or work.
turns.tutor: Hello! Great idea. Rules are things you must do or must not do. For example: "You must wear a seatbelt in a car." Can you tell me one rule at your school or work?

turns.learner: At work you must come at nine o'clock. And you mustn't bring lunch, because the company gives you lunch.
turns.tutor: "You must come at nine" is perfect! But careful: "mustn't" means forbidden, like a strong "no". If lunch is free, it is not necessary to bring it. We say "You don't have to bring lunch." Can you try again?

turns.learner: I am confused. I thought mustn't and don't have to are the same. Both mean not necessary, no?
turns.tutor: Good question! They are different. "Mustn't" = forbidden: "You mustn't shout in a hospital" (shouting is not allowed). "Don't have to" = not necessary: "You don't have to pay to enter the park" (you can pay or not). Which one means "not allowed"?

turns.learner: Mustn't means not allowed, in the hospital example. Maybe don't have to also? I am not sure.
turns.tutor: Yes, mustn't = not allowed. Well done! But "don't have to" is NOT "not allowed". It means you have a choice. Free lunch: you don't have to bring lunch, but you can. Try: "In a library you ___ shout."

turns.learner: In a library you mustn't shout. It is not allowed. And free lunch, I don't have to bring it. OK.
turns.tutor: Excellent! Both sentences are correct. Now a new one: It is a holiday, so you ___ go to school. It is not necessary. Which word fits: must, mustn't, or don't have to?

turns.learner: It is a holiday so you mustn't go to school. Not necessary.
turns.tutor: Nice try, but "mustn't" means forbidden. On a holiday school is not forbidden, it is just not necessary. So: "You don't have to go to school." Remember: mustn't = not allowed; don't have to = not necessary.
